content: Miscarriage refers to the natural or spontaneous termination of a pregnancy at a stage where the embryo or fetus is not viable, typically defined in humans as occurring before 20 weeks of gestation. It is the most common complication of early pregnancy. The medical term spontaneous abortion is used to describe miscarriages because the term abortion in medical contexts refers to any terminated pregnancy, whether induced or spontaneous. However, in common language, abortion is often associated specifically with the deliberate termination of pregnancy. When examining the pathological features of a miscarriage, both gross and microscopic findings are evaluated. Microscopic examination may reveal the presence of products of conception, including villi, trophoblast tissue, fetal parts, and gestational changes in the endometrium. Genetic testing can also be conducted to identify abnormal chromosomal arrangements that may have contributed to the miscarriage. The most common symptom of a miscarriage is vaginal bleeding. Bleeding during pregnancy is often referred to as a threatened abortion. Among women who seek medical attention for bleeding during pregnancy, approximately half will experience a miscarriage. Other symptoms, apart from bleeding, are not statistically associated with an increased risk of miscarriage. Surgical treatment, most commonly vacuum aspiration (sometimes referred to as dilation and curettage, or D&C, and dilation and evacuation, or D&E), is the fastest method to complete the miscarriage process. This approach reduces the duration and severity of bleeding and is the most effective treatment for physical pain associated with miscarriage. In cases of recurrent miscarriage or pregnancy loss in later stages, D&C is also the preferred method for obtaining tissue samples for pathological examination.
